result.summary: Arete persuades Alcinous to judge that Medea stays with Jason if already wed, and the Argonauts hasten the marriage in a sacred cave. After leaving Drepane they are blown into the Syrtis in Libya, where they despair until Libyan heroine-nymphs give a riddling message, a sea-horse appears, and they carry the Argo overland to the Tritonian lake and the garden of the Hesperides.

scenes.title: Arete pleads for Medea
scenes.summary: Arete begs Alcinous to protect Medea; he rules she returns to her father only if still a maiden. Arete secretly sends her herald to tell Jason to marry.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks being handed back to Aeetes and his wrath.

scenes.title: Wedding in the sacred cave
scenes.summary: The heroes receive the message, sacrifice and prepare the bridal bed in Macris' cave with the fleece, with nymphs and Orpheus' song.
scenes.stakes: Jason and Medea fear Alcinous' sentence may not be upheld.

scenes.title: Alcinous' judgement and departure
scenes.summary: Alcinous publicly confirms the marriage, and the Colchians submit and settle. The Argonauts depart with gifts and twelve handmaids.
scenes.stakes: Alcinous risks war with Aeetes by upholding his judgement.

scenes.title: Stranded in the Syrtis
scenes.summary: A north wind drives the Argo into the Syrtis shoals; Ancaeus despairs and the crew lie down to die.
scenes.stakes: The whole crew faces death by thirst and stranding with no way back.

scenes.title: Libyan heroines and the horse
scenes.summary: Libyan nymphs tell Jason to rouse his comrades; a golden-maned horse leaps from the sea, and Peleus interprets it as a guide.
scenes.stakes: The crew will die unless they decipher the message and find a way to water.

scenes.title: Carrying the Argo to Hesperides
scenes.summary: The narrator tells how the heroes carried the ship twelve days to the Tritonian lake and found the dead serpent Ladon; Orpheus prays to the vanished Hesperides.

notable_quotes.reason: Narrator's reflection that bitterness accompanies every human joy.

analysis.text: Law, fatherly power and divine guidance shape the marriage and the trials; endurance is rewarded when the heroes interpret omens.
The Corcyra setting and the mention of the Bacchiadae reflect Greek colonial history that Apollonius ties to myth.

fun_facts.text: The Syrtis was a feared real stretch of shoals and quicksand on the Libyan coast known to ancient sailors.

language_notes.text: "Aforetime" means previously or as before; "lay" here means rested in bed.
The Minyae are Jason's crew, named for the Minyans, the ancestral people from whom many of the Argonauts descended.
Haemonia is an old name for Thessaly, Jason's homeland; "Argos" here is the name of the ship Argo, not the city.
"To cure one ill by another" means she escaped the consequence of her first wrong (helping Jason) by committing a second, fleeing her father.
Nycteus, Antiope's father, persecuted her after Zeus fathered children on her; she fled and suffered cruelty from him and later his kin.
Danae's father Acrisius set her and her infant Perseus adrift in a chest on the sea.
Echetus was a legendary cruel king, said to have blinded his daughter and set her to grind bronze grains as an impossible task.
Zeus guarded oaths and suppliants; Alcinous fears offending him by breaking the sanctity of Medea's supplication.
The verdict hinges on whether the marriage has been consummated; a wife's bond was held to override her father's claim.
"Fair-omened" means promising good fortune.
"Mingled a bowl" refers to mixing wine with water in a mixing bowl for libations to the gods, the normal Greek custom.
"Straightway" is an archaic word meaning immediately.
The Nysean son of Zeus is Dionysus, rescued from the flame when his mother Semele was destroyed; Hermes carried the infant away.
The Phaeacians' land is Scheria, home of Alcinous; the cave there is identified with Macris' retreat after Hera exiled her from Euboea.
"Minded to complete his marriage" means he intended the wedding to be consummated; he preferred to do so properly at home in Ioleus.
The sentence of Alcinous: he ruled that if Medea was still a maiden she must return to her father, but if already wed she could stay with Jason.
"By reason of his covenant" means because of the agreement he had made earlier, to judge between Jason's party and the Colchians.
"Jars of wine for mixing" refers to the Greek custom of diluting wine with water in a large bowl before drinking.
"As women will" is the narrator's aside: women customarily brought linen and ornaments as wedding gifts.
The Bacchiadae were a Corinthian ruling clan; Ephyra is an old name for Corinth. The poet refers to later Greek settlement of Corcyra.
The poet points to a cult site that still existed in his own day, linking the myth to a real place and practice.
Drepane is the Phaeacians' island, later identified with Corcyra (Corfu).
"Howbeit" means 'however'; Achaea here means Greece. The heroes must first endure Libya before reaching home.
The places listed (Ambracian gulf, Curetes' land, Echinades, Pelops' land, the Peloponnese) trace the Greek west coast, showing the Argo almost home before being blown off course.
Syrtis is the dangerous shallow gulf on the North African coast (modern Gulf of Sidra), notorious in antiquity for trapping ships.
The clashing rocks are the Symplegades, which the Argo had already passed earlier in the voyage.
"Let him sit at the helm the man..." is a bitter invitation: Ancaeus gives up the steering to anyone who thinks he can do better.
Sweating, bleeding images and bellowing temples are omens of disaster that ancient people feared; so is the sun darkening at midday.
Pactolus is a river in Lydia (Asia Minor), proverbial for swans and its golden sands.
Athena was born fully armed from the head of her father Zeus; the Libyan nymphs claim to have first bathed her at Lake Trito.
Riddling oracle: the 'mother' who bore them is the Argo, and Amphitrite unyoking Poseidon's horses signals the moment to carry the ship overland.
'If haply' means 'in case perhaps'; Jason hopes they can find a sign of how to escape.
Minyae: the Argonauts, named after the Minyans, ancestors of many of the heroes.
'I ween' is archaic for 'I think' or 'I suppose'.
The Pierides are the Muses, named from Pieria, their cult home; the poet claims them as his source.
Ladon guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides; Heracles killed him in his eleventh labour, just before the Argonauts arrive.
Heracles' arrows were poisoned with the Lernaean hydra's gall, which is why the serpent's wounds fester and kill flies.

context_notes.text: Alcinous and Arete rule the Phaeacians on Drepane. Arete was notably honored, and her influence over her husband is stressed here.
Arete secretly arranges the wedding so Alcinous's own ruling will protect Medea; the heralds served as trusted messengers.
Aristaeus was a minor god credited with beekeeping and olive cultivation; his daughter Macris nursed the infant Dionysus.
Hera was the jealous wife of Zeus and persecuted children he had by other women, including Dionysus.
Orpheus was the legendary musician of the Argonauts; singing the marriage song (hymenaeus) at the bridal chamber door was a Greek custom.
Alcinous is king of the Phaeacians; a staff of justice marked a king's authority as judge.
The son of Oeagrus is Orpheus, the legendary singer and lyre-player sailing with the Argonauts.
Hera, goddess of marriage, protects Jason's cause throughout the poem. Arete is Alcinous' queen, who had urged the marriage.
The Minyae is a name for the Argonauts, many being descended from the Minyans of Orchomenus and Iolcus.
Ancaeus is the Argo's helmsman, taking over after Tiphys died earlier in the voyage.
The maidens are the Colchian women given to Medea by her; the daughter of Aeetes is Medea.
Jason has lain down covered by his cloak in despair, stranded in the Libyan desert with the Argo cut off from the sea.
Peleus, father of Achilles, is one of the Argonauts; here he solves the riddle.
The Hesperides are nymphs who tend the golden apples in the far west, near Atlas, who holds up the sky.

literary_notes.text: Arete cites mythical fathers' cruelty as precedents, strengthening her plea by placing Aeetes in a familiar pattern of paternal wrath.
The vivid, grim picture of grinding bronze in darkness heightens the pathos and the danger Medea faces.
The brief, quiet closing of his speech marks the scene's turn from the couple's talk to Arete's covert action.
Arete's immediate secret action shows her as shrewd and decisive, working through her husband's own judgment.
The fleece's glow is compared to flame, making the golden wool a dazzling, almost supernatural object.
Awe is described as actively holding the nymphs back, giving the fleece's sacred power a restraining force.
The narrator steps in with a general reflection on mortal life, shifting from story to commentary and darkening the celebration.
Their fear of Alcinous' verdict hints at uncertainty even amid the joyful wedding, preparing the reader for the coming tension.
The island beaches "laughed out" at dawn, giving the landscape joy that matches the mood of the coming wedding.
The narrator turns directly to Hera, "in thy honour," crediting her divine influence over events.
Alcinous is shown as fearless and just, holding to his oaths despite Aeetes' threatened wrath.
The narrator leaps ahead to the later fate of the Colchians, a long view typical of this poet's voice.
Repeated 'on every hand' and the picture of still sand with nothing moving build a sense of lifeless desolation.
The crew now wishes they had risked the Clashing Rocks, a danger they once feared most, showing how bad their present state seems.
The stunned heroes are compared to men wandering a city waiting for catastrophe and omens, conveying their dread and numbness.
The weeping women are likened first to abandoned chicks, then to singing swans, joining helplessness with mournful beauty.
Jason's shout is compared to a roaring lion that terrifies herdsmen, contrasted with the comfort it brings his friends.
The golden-maned horse rising from the sea acts as a divine sign and guide, linked to Poseidon.
The poet steps forward, invoking the Muses and addressing the heroes directly, which lends authority to the marvellous feat.
The exclamations about the long carry stress the heroes' superhuman endurance.
Likening the thirsty heroes to raging hounds conveys their desperate, animal need for water.
The Hesperides, lamenting the serpent, vanish into dust as the heroes approach, frustrating their hope of help.
